title: Brokers, Prop Firms & Accounts
hook: Know the difference before you fund an account.
mission: By the end of this lesson, you should be able to explain what a broker account, a prop firm evaluation, and a simulated account each actually test.

blocks.heading: Every account is either your money, someone else's money, or practice money

beats.heading: A broker account
beats.body: Trades your own personal capital — you keep every dollar of profit and absorb every dollar of loss yourself.

beats.heading: A prop firm evaluation
beats.body: Gives you access to their capital if you can prove you can trade within their rules first; once funded, profits are usually split.

beats.heading: A simulated account
beats.body: Uses no real money at all — it exists purely to practice execution without financial risk.

blocks.heading: Match the account to the goal
sequence: A trader wants to test whether her execution is consistent before risking real money
blocks.askAfter: A trader wants to test whether her execution is consistent before risking real money
blocks.prompt: Which account type actually answers that question?

options.label: A simulated (demo) account
options.feedback: Right — simulated accounts exist to prove consistency with zero financial risk.

options.label: Jump straight to a funded account
options.feedback: Skipping straight to funded capital without proving consistency first is a real risk.

blocks.quote: I'm not telling you which account type to start with. I'm telling you to know exactly which one you're in, and what that account expects from you, before you place a single trade.

questions.question: A trader passes a prop firm's evaluation and gets funded. Whose capital is she now trading, and what does that change about her risk?
options: The firm's capital — her personal money isn't directly at risk, but she now trades inside the firm's rules
Her own capital — the evaluation was just a formality
Nobody's capital — funded accounts are simulated
questions.why: Funded status shifts whose money is at risk but adds real rule constraints in exchange.

questions.question: A prop firm's evaluation exists to test whether a trader can follow ___ before the firm gives her access to its capital.
questions.why: Rule-discipline is proven first — capital access comes after.

blocks.prompt: Imagine another AGHF girl asks: "Should I just go straight for a funded prop account?" How would you explain the trade-offs to her?

takeaways: A broker account risks your own capital from trade one.
A prop evaluation tests rule-discipline before granting capital access.
A simulated account proves consistency with zero financial risk.
remember: Know exactly which account you're in, and what it expects from you.
